# Imports
```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
```



# A six-sided die is rolled repeatedly. What is the expected value average as the die is rolled more and more? The expected value for a single roll is 1+2+3+4+5+6 / 6 = 3.5. What’s wrong with the answer, just in logical terms? Create this in R (i.e., simulate many rolls and visualize the results).
```{r}
rolls <- 10000 # number of rolls
die_rolls <- sample(1:6, rolls, replace = TRUE) # simulate rolling a die 10,000 times
die_rolls_df <- data.frame(roll = die_rolls) # create a dataframe for visualization
# Die have whole numbers, such as 1, 2, 3. Just because the average is 3.5 does not mean you will roll a 3.5 because 3.5 is not the side of a die. The average value will approach 3.5 as the number of rolls increases, but it will never actually be 3.5.

mean(die_rolls_df$roll) # for example, this was 3.48

roll_counts <- table(die_rolls_df$roll)
barplot(roll_counts,
  main = "Frequency of Die Rolls (1–6)",
  xlab = "Die Face",
  ylab = "Count",
  col = "skyblue",
  border = "white"
)
```


# A box contains 30 red balls and 15 green balls. A ball is drawn from the box, and the color is written down. The ball is then returned to the box, and the process is repeated. What is the expected proportion of red balls drawn as the number of draws increases? Create this in R (i.e., simulate the draws from the box and visualize the results).

```{r}
balls_drawn <- 100000 # number of balls drawn
balls <- sample(c("red", "green"), rolls, replace = TRUE, prob = c(2 / 3, 1 / 3))
balls_df <- data.frame(draw = balls) # create a dataframe for visualization

draw_counts <- table(balls_df$draw)


barplot(draw_counts,
  main = "Frequency of Drawing a Ball (Red or Green)",
  xlab = "Ball Color",
  ylab = "Count",
  col = "skyblue",
  border = "white"
)

theoretical_red_to_green_ratio <- 30 / 15 # 2:1
actual_red_to_green_ratio <- draw_counts["red"] / draw_counts["green"]

cat(paste(
  "Expected ratio of red to green balls:", theoretical_red_to_green_ratio,
  "\nActual ratio of red to green balls:", round(actual_red_to_green_ratio, 2)
))
```

# Do Exercise 1 from the text (in Chapter 9). You can use the author’s code, and it is strongly suggested that instead of copying/pasting, you re-write the code. Explain each line in the code both in programming (i.e., what the R is doing) and statistics terms.
```{r}
# Cohen's imports
library(ggplot2)
library(cowplot)
library(emg)
library(pracma)
library(tidyr)

theme_set(theme_classic(base_size = 14))
options(scipen = 999)


N <- 500 # number of iterations
nSamples <- 50 # number of samples
kHistBins <- 20 # number of histogram bins, this is useful for limiting the values we plot

# creates a sequence of numbers from -3 to 3
edges <- seq(-3, 3, length.out = kHistBins + 1) # create edges for the histogram bins

# creates matrix of 0 with samples and bins
allHistY <- matrix(0, nrow = nSamples, ncol = kHistBins)
allMeans <- rep(0, nSamples) # create a vector to store means of each sample
ldatall <- data.frame(mids = NULL, Count = NULL) # empty data frame with two column

for (sampi in 1:nSamples) { # this was much cleaner for looping
  data <- rnorm(N, mean = 0, sd = 1) # generate random normal data
  histY <- hist(data[abs(data) <= 3.0], breaks = edges, plot = FALSE) # create histogram data
  allHistY[sampi, ] <- histY$counts # store histogram counts
  ldat <- data.frame(mids = histY$mids, Count = histY$counts) # create a dataframe for the histogram
  allMeans[sampi] <- mean(data) # calculate the mean of the data
  ldatall <- rbind(ldatall, ldat) # combine all histograms into one dataframe
}

titleA <- expression(paste(bold("A)"), " Histograms")) # title for the first plot
titleB <- bquote(bold("B)") ~ "Scatter of means (mean=" ~ .(sprintf("%.3g", mean(allMeans))) * ")") # title for the second plot
# generates 50 random numbers from a uniform distribution between 0.5 and 0.9.
c <- runif(50, min = 0.5, max = 0.9)

# create the first plot showing all histogram points from all samples
ggp1 <- ggplot(data = ldatall) + # use the combined histogram data
  aes(x = mids, y = Count) + # set x to bin midpoints and y to counts
  theme(legend.position = "none") + # remove legend for a cleaner look
  geom_point( # plot each point as a dot
    colour = rgb(rep(c, 20), rep(c, 20), rep(c, 20)), # use grayscale colors for each sample
    size = 3.5 # set point size
  ) +
  geom_line( # add a line summarizing all samples
    stat = "summary", # use summary statistics (mean by default)
    fun = "mean", # plot the mean count at each x
    linewidth = 1.5 # set line thickness
  ) +
  labs( # add axis labels and title
    x = "Data value",
    y = "Count",
    title = titleA
  ) +
  theme( # more custom theming?
    axis.text = element_text(size = 14),
    plot.title = element_text(vjust = -1)
  )

# create the second plot showing the sample means from all 50 samples
ggp2 <- ggplot() +
  geom_point( # plot each sample mean as a filled square
    aes(x = 1:50, y = allMeans), # x-axis: sample number, y-axis: sample mean
    shape = 22, # use filled square shape
    size = 5, # set size of the squares?
    fill = rgb(c, c, c), # use same grayscale values as in ggp1
    stroke = 1.0
  ) +
  geom_hline( # add a horizontal dashed line at the overall mean of sample means
    yintercept = mean(allMeans), # position at the mean of all sample means
    linetype = 2,
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  labs( # add axis labels and title
    x = "Sample number",
    y = "Sample mean",
    title = titleB
  ) +
  theme( # adjust visual appearance
    legend.position = "none", # no legend
    axis.text = element_text(size = 14), # larger axis text
    plot.title = element_text(vjust = -1) # adjust vertical title position
  )

# combine the two plots vertically into one figure
plot_grid(ggp1, ggp2, ncol = 1, align = "v")
```
